name: Drab Green
lede: Drab Green is a muted, mid-toned olive green, a crowd name from the 2010 xkcd color survey built on an old English word for dullness.

sections.title: Drab, borrowed for a green
sections.body:
The only recorded source for Drab Green is the xkcd survey of 2010 [1]. *Drab* on its own is centuries older than that. Paterson's dictionary uses it for a plain, dull color with no brightness, a word historically tied to undyed wool cloth [1]. Our library separately carries it as half of [[drab-grey|Drab Grey]], first set down in Ridgway's 1886 atlas [1]. Drab Green pairs that same plain word with [[green]], rather than continuing any formal naming system [1].

At hex #749551 it measures lightness 58 and chroma 40 in LCH, and the nearest ISCC-NBS block reads as a moderate yellow green, 4.6 units off [1]. Its closest named neighbor is [[flat-green|Flat Green]], 4.0 units away and more vivid, followed by [[swedish-green|Swedish Green]], 4.4 units off, also more vivid [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This match appears in 0.35% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive (84 paintings, as photographed); the within-painting lens narrows that to 36 [3]. In our archive it is rarer than 55% of the named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 0.7% of the 1,674 paintings we have from that decade (12 paintings), 3.9 times the rate its museums would predict [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent across its 36 appearances by lightness rank within the painting [3]. It is most over-represented in France, 2.4x expected (17 of 3,443 paintings) [3]. The earliest match dates to 1512, 498 years before the name's 2010 record, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin and a look-alike hue in an aged photograph is not proof of a pigment or dye [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so the match is a screen comparison, not a pigment identification [3].
